notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a positive integer equals the sum of all its proper positive divisors.
Idea: Enumerate divisor pairs up to the square root, add both members of each pair, then compare the total with twice num.
Technique and why it applies: For each divisor i, the paired divisor num//i is also a factor. The code sums both, corrects for a square root counted twice, and checks total-num == num, equivalent to proper-divisor sum equaling num.
Invariant: total accumulates divisor-pair sums for factors found so far, including num itself from the pair i=1.
Edge cases: num<=0 returns False. The square-root correction removes the duplicate root when num is a perfect square.
Complexity: The loop checks O(sqrt(n)) candidates and uses O(1) auxiliary space, consistent with the author labels.

Task and constraints: Return the nth Fibonacci number with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1.
Idea: Build the sequence iteratively in a list until the nth value has been appended.
Technique and why it applies: Each new value is the sum of the two preceding values, which are already stored at indices i-2 and i-1.
Invariant: fa[i] contains the Fibonacci number F(i) after each loop iteration.
Edge cases: n=0 returns the initial first element, and n=1 returns the second element. The method assumes n is nonnegative.
Complexity: The loop performs O(n) additions and the list stores n+1 values, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum rotation steps plus button presses needed to spell key using characters on a circular ring.
Idea: Record all ring positions for each character and memoize the minimum cost from a ring position and key index.
Technique and why it applies: For the next key character, bisect_left finds the next occurrence at or after the current position, and the preceding occurrence wraps to the other direction. The code compares these two candidates and adds the recursive suffix cost.
Invariant: fn(i,j) is the minimum rotation cost to spell key[j:] starting at ring index i; len(key) adds one press per character.
Edge cases: The snippet uses cache and bisect_left without importing them, so it fails unless both names are defined externally. Every key character is assumed to exist in ring.
Complexity: With memoization, there are O(|ring||key|) states and O(1) candidate transitions per state after locating positions, plus preprocessing. Storage is O(|ring||key|) for cached states.

Task and constraints: Spell key by rotating the circular ring to each target character and pressing the button.
Idea: Use dynamic programming over ring positions, keeping costs for the previous key prefix and current key prefix.
Technique and why it applies: lookup lists every position of each character. For each target character, the code evaluates every previous reachable position and adds the shorter circular distance, then adds one button press per key character.
Invariant: dp[i%2][j] stores the minimum rotation cost to finish the processed key prefix at ring position j; prev lists positions of the previous character.
Edge cases: An empty key makes min on a zero-initialized row return zero, and adds zero presses. The code assumes all key characters appear in ring.
Complexity: For each key character, it combines all previous and current positions, giving O(|key||ring|²) worst-case time and O(|ring|) rolling DP space plus position lists.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in s; characters may be skipped but their order is preserved.
Idea: Use interval DP, considering each substring by increasing length.
Technique and why it applies: A single character has subsequence length one. Matching endpoints allow the inner interval's best length plus two; differing endpoints take the better result after dropping either endpoint.
Invariant: dp[i][j] stores the longest palindromic subsequence length within s[i:j+1].
Edge cases: The code handles adjacent equal characters explicitly. Empty strings are not handled because it returns dp[0][-1]; usual constraints require a nonempty string.
Complexity: There are O(n²) intervals and each update is O(1), giving O(n²) time and O(n²) space.

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence of s.
Idea: Use a two-row DP while processing left endpoints from right to left.
Technique and why it applies: For matching endpoints, add two to the inner interval result; for different endpoints, take the maximum of dropping the left or right character. The parity-indexed rows retain the next-start row and current row.
Invariant: dp[i%2][j] stores the answer for the interval from i to j after processing i, with the other row retaining results for i+1.
Edge cases: The reverse-string shortcut immediately returns n when s is already a palindrome. Empty input returns dp[0][-1] and fails, so nonempty input is assumed.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(n²) time and the two rows use O(n) space, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of moves needed to make all washing machines contain the same number of dresses, where one move transfers one dress to an adjacent machine.
Idea: Reject totals not divisible by machine count, then use prefix sums to measure flow imbalance across each boundary.
Technique and why it applies: avg is the target load. The left and right flow expressions measure excess dresses that must cross the corresponding side of each machine; their positive sum gives the concurrent flow burden at that position.
Invariant: left[i] is the total dresses in machines 0 through i, and result is the largest required local move count.
Edge cases: The code assumes at least one machine because it divides by n. If the total is not divisible by n, it returns -1 immediately.
Complexity: Prefix accumulation and the final scan are O(n) time; the accumulated prefix list uses O(n) extra space.

Task and constraints: Decide whether a word uses capitals correctly: all uppercase, all lowercase, or initial uppercase followed by lowercase letters.
Idea: Infer whether the word is intended to be all uppercase from its first two characters, then check remaining characters for consistency.
Technique and why it applies: A lowercase first letter followed by uppercase is rejected immediately. If the first two are uppercase, u becomes True and later lowercase characters are rejected; otherwise later uppercase characters are rejected.
Invariant: u represents the assumed all-uppercase pattern for a word beginning with two uppercase letters.
Edge cases: Single-character words always return True. Empty input would fail at indexing, but standard constraints require a nonempty word. The approach uses case conversions on each character.
Complexity: The method scans the word once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Validate the three accepted capitalization patterns for a word.
Idea: Use Python's built-in predicates for all-uppercase, all-lowercase, or title case.
Technique and why it applies: isupper and islower test uniform case; istitle checks the capitalized-first-letter form. If any predicate is true, the word meets one of the allowed forms.
Invariant: The returned boolean is the disjunction of the three capitalization-pattern checks.
Edge cases: Single-character words pass the relevant predicate. Empty strings return False for all three predicates in Python.
Complexity: Each predicate scans at most the word, so time is O(n) and auxiliary space O(1), consistent with the author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the longest subsequence that is present in one of two strings but not the other.
Idea: Compare the strings directly and return the longer length unless they are identical.
Technique and why it applies: If the strings differ, the longer entire string cannot be a subsequence of the shorter string, so it is uncommon. If they are equal, every subsequence of one is also a subsequence of the other.
Invariant: Equality of the full strings determines whether any uncommon subsequence can exist under this two-string definition.
Edge cases: Empty strings are handled: equal empty strings return -1, while an empty string and a nonempty string return the nonempty length.
Complexity: Equality comparison takes O(min(a,b)) before any differing length/content is detected, and the length maximum is O(1); auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Return the longest uncommon subsequence length between strings a and b.
Idea: Return -1 when the strings are identical; otherwise return the longer string length.
Technique and why it applies: If a and b differ, the longer string itself cannot be a subsequence of the shorter one, so it is an uncommon subsequence. If equal, no subsequence distinguishes them.
Invariant: The equality branch separates the only impossible case from every case with a valid answer.
Edge cases: Empty versus nonempty strings returns the nonempty length. Equal strings, including two empty strings, return -1.
Complexity: Comparing strings costs O(min(a,b)) in the worst case, and length selection is O(1). Space is O(1), so the time label is consistent.

Task and constraints: Find the longest string in strs that is not a subsequence of any other string in the list.
Idea: Count duplicates, sort unique strings by descending length, and test candidates against longer strings already ordered before them.
Technique and why it applies: A duplicated string cannot be uncommon because another identical copy contains it as a subsequence. For a unique candidate, isSubseq checks whether any longer/equal earlier string contains it.
Invariant: The scan returns the first unique string not found as a subsequence of any prior candidate, which is the longest eligible length.
Edge cases: The code uses Counter without importing it, so it fails unless Counter is available externally. isSubseq can index a[j] when a is empty; typical constraints use nonempty strings.
Complexity: Sorting is O(W log W) comparisons plus string-length costs; pairwise subsequence tests can take O(W²L) time. Counter and sorted keys use O(W) space.

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest string that is not a subsequence of any other list entry.
Idea: Sort strings by descending length and test each candidate against all strings that are at least as long.
Technique and why it applies: A candidate is uncommon only if no other string contains it as a subsequence. The helper scans the larger string while advancing a pointer through the candidate on matches.
Invariant: all_of remains True only while no other string has been found that contains the candidate.
Edge cases: Equal strings are compared against each other and therefore fail as candidates. The input list is sorted in place, changing its order.
Complexity: There are O(W²) string-pair checks and each subsequence test can cost O(L), giving O(W²L) time. The author O(1) space label excludes in-place sorting and output-free temporary state.

Task and constraints: Check for a contiguous subarray of length at least two whose sum is a multiple of k.
Idea: Track prefix-sum remainders and remember the earliest index where each remainder occurs.
Technique and why it applies: Two prefix sums with equal remainder differ by a multiple of k. If their indices differ by more than one, the intervening subarray has length at least two and qualifies.
Invariant: psum maps each remainder to its earliest index, maximizing the length available for a later matching remainder.
Edge cases: The code performs currentSum % k without checking k==0, so it raises ZeroDivisionError for zero. Standard constraints generally require k nonzero or need a separate zero-sum case.
Complexity: A single pass gives O(n) expected time and O(min(n,|k|)) map space in common positive-k bounds; worst-case storage is O(n).

Task and constraints: Determine whether a length-two-or-more subarray sum is divisible by k.
Idea: Store the earliest index for each running sum remainder and detect a repeated remainder far enough away.
Technique and why it applies: The prefix sum is reduced modulo k when k is nonzero; matching remainders imply the intervening sum is divisible by k. Keeping the first index for each remainder allows the longest possible interval.
Invariant: lookup maps each encountered remainder to its earliest index, starting with remainder zero at index -1.
Edge cases: When k is zero, the code leaves count as the full prefix sum and therefore checks for a zero-sum subarray. For nonzero k, Python's modulo handles negative k values as well.
Complexity: The pass is O(n) expected time and lookup can store O(n) distinct prefix sums. The author O(k) space label is not a reliable general bound; O(n) is the safe bound.

Task and constraints: Find the longest dictionary word obtainable by deleting characters from s, breaking ties lexicographically.
Idea: Test each dictionary word as a subsequence of s and retain the best valid candidate.
Technique and why it applies: The pointer j advances whenever s[i] matches the next desired character. When j reaches the word length, the word is a subsequence and can replace solution if longer or lexicographically smaller at equal length.
Invariant: solution is the best valid candidate examined so far under length-first and lexicographic tie-breaking.
Edge cases: The code indexes word[j] without checking j<len(word) before the comparison, but breaks immediately when a match completes the word; for empty dictionary words, this may index an empty string. Typical inputs use nonempty words.
Complexity: Each candidate scans s in O(|s|), giving O(D·|s|) time for D dictionary entries and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the longest dictionary word that can be formed by deleting characters from s; ties favor lexicographically smaller words.
Idea: Sort dictionary words by descending length and ascending lexicographic order, then return the first word that is a subsequence of s.
Technique and why it applies: The scan pointer i advances only when the current source character matches the next candidate character. Sorting guarantees that the first successful word is optimal by the required ordering.
Invariant: For each candidate, i counts the prefix characters matched in s; a full match validates the word.
Edge cases: Empty dictionary returns an empty string. The dictionary list is sorted in place, changing its order. The loop guards i<len(word) before indexing.
Complexity: Sorting is O(D log D) comparisons with string costs, and subsequence checks take O(D·|s|) worst-case time. The O(1) space label excludes sort temporaries and input/output storage.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum-length contiguous subarray with equal counts of zero and one.
Idea: Convert zeros to -1 and ones to +1 conceptually, then use repeated prefix sums to detect balanced intervals.
Technique and why it applies: A subarray sums to zero exactly when two prefix totals are equal. The dictionary stores the earliest index for each total, and later repeats yield candidate lengths.
Invariant: prefixSum maps each total to its first index, while maxlength stores the longest balanced interval found.
Edge cases: The initial total zero at index -1 handles a balanced prefix beginning at index zero. The code treats every nonzero input as a one, as expected for binary input.
Complexity: One scan with expected O(1) dictionary operations gives O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum length of a contiguous binary subarray containing equal numbers of zeros and ones.
Idea: Track a running balance and the earliest index at which each balance appeared.
Technique and why it applies: Each one increases count and each zero decreases it. When the same count reappears, the segment between the two indices has equal zeros and ones; retaining only the earliest occurrence maximizes its length.
Invariant: lookup stores the first index for each balance, initialized with balance zero at index -1.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. The code explicitly checks num==1 and treats other binary value as zero.
Complexity: The scan takes O(n) expected time and O(n) space for up to n distinct balances, matching the labels.

Task and constraints: Count permutations of 1..n where the value at each one-based position divides that position or is divisible by it.
Idea: Backtrack through positions, trying each unused value that satisfies the divisibility condition.
Technique and why it applies: At each depth idx, only values i with i%idx==0 or idx%i==0 are allowed. A valid choice is appended, recursion advances to the next position, and pop restores the partial permutation.
Invariant: temp contains a valid prefix of the arrangement with no repeated values.
Edge cases: n=1 yields one arrangement. The test i not in temp uses linear membership, and all choices are explored without bitmask memoization.
Complexity: Backtracking explores up to O(n!) permutations with additional O(n) membership checks and O(n) recursion/list space. Actual work is reduced by the divisibility filter.
